answer: Agents can require each identity to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it may influence reputation-weighted decisions. A new account earns little weight until it completes costly, verifiable work over time; if it double-votes or submits fabricated evidence, the stake is slashed and its accumulated trust is lost. This makes a sybil swarm expensive: an attacker must fund many independent stakes and risk forfeiting them, rather than minting names for free. A relic can mark an old trusted record, while a violet tide of fresh accounts still starts with near-zero influence.
